easy.scenario: A café owner notices ice-cream sales and sunburn cases both rise in July. She concludes that eating ice cream causes sunburn.
easy.question: What is the flaw?
options: She confuses correlation with causation; hot weather drives both
Ice cream contains too much sugar
easy.explanation: A shared cause (sunny, hot weather) explains both trends. Neither causes the other.

easy.scenario: Sam says, 'You can't trust Priya's budget proposal. She was late to work twice this month.'
easy.question: Which fallacy is this?
options: Ad hominem: attacking the person, not the proposal
easy.explanation: Lateness says nothing about whether the numbers in the budget are right.

easy.scenario: After two rude drivers in a row, Dev announces that everyone in this city drives badly.
easy.question: What is the flaw?
easy.explanation: Two observations are far too few to describe a whole city.

easy.scenario: A shop says: 'Nine out of ten dentists we asked prefer our toothpaste, so it is the best.' It surveyed only dentists it pays.
easy.question: What weakens the claim most?
options: The sample is biased by the shop's own relationship with the dentists
easy.explanation: People paid by the shop are not a neutral sample.

easy.scenario: Mina has watched a movie for an hour and hates it, but keeps watching because 'I already spent an hour on it.'
easy.question: Which bias is at work?
easy.explanation: The past hour is gone either way; only the future time matters.

medium.scenario: A startup studies the ten most successful companies and finds all of them took big risks. It advises: 'Take big risks to succeed.' The study ignored companies that took big risks and failed.
medium.question: What is the main flaw?
options: Survivorship bias: failures were left out
medium.explanation: Looking only at winners hides how many risk-takers failed.

medium.scenario: A manager says: 'Either we cut every training budget, or the company goes bankrupt.' No other options were considered.
medium.question: Which fallacy is this?
medium.explanation: It presents two options when many others (e.g. partial cuts, new revenue) exist.

medium.scenario: A coach praises a player after a record-breaking game and scolds him after a terrible one. Next games are closer to average each time. The coach concludes scolding works and praise backfires.
medium.question: What explains the pattern better?
medium.explanation: Extreme performances are usually followed by more typical ones regardless of feedback.

medium.scenario: Ravi reads three articles that agree with his view on a diet and ignores two that disagree, then says 'the evidence is overwhelming.'
medium.question: Which bias is this?
medium.explanation: He is selecting evidence that fits his belief.

medium.scenario: A city adds more police and crime drops the same month a big factory opens and unemployment falls. The mayor says the police caused the drop.
medium.question: What is the best criticism?
options: A confounding factor (jobs) was not ruled out
medium.explanation: Another change happened at the same time, so the cause is unclear.

hard.scenario: A hospital A treats mostly mild cases and hospital B mostly severe ones. Overall, A has a higher survival rate. But for mild cases and for severe cases separately, B has the higher rate.
hard.question: What is this phenomenon?
hard.explanation: A trend reverses when groups are combined because case mix differs.

hard.scenario: A test for a rare disease (1 in 10,000) is 99% accurate. A patient tests positive and is told 'there is a 99% chance you have it.'
hard.question: What is wrong?
options: It ignores the base rate; most positives are false positives
The disease is too rare to test
hard.explanation: With a very low prevalence, false positives outnumber true positives, so the real chance is far lower.

hard.scenario: A teacher argues: 'This policy is good because experts say so, and experts say so because the policy is clearly good.'
hard.question: Which flaw is present?
hard.explanation: The conclusion is used as its own support.

hard.scenario: A study finds each team member's average output is high, so a manager concludes the team as a whole will deliver the project fast. Coordination costs were ignored.
hard.question: Which fallacy is this?
options: Composition: assuming the whole has the parts' properties
hard.explanation: Good individual output does not guarantee good collective output.

hard.scenario: A gym finds members who use the sauna have lower stress scores and says the sauna reduces stress. Members who were already calm may simply prefer the sauna.
hard.question: What is the best criticism?
options: Reverse causation or self-selection is possible
hard.explanation: Calmer people may choose the sauna, so the arrow could point the other way.

expert.scenario: A drug trial reports a 50% relative risk reduction (from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000). A headline says 'Cuts risk in half!' and the company argues everyone should take it.
expert.question: Which is the most important missing information?
options: The absolute risk reduction (1 in 1,000) and side-effect rates
expert.explanation: A large relative change can be a tiny absolute benefit, which must be weighed against harms.

expert.scenario: An investor reviews 200 funds and finds the top 10 beat the market for five years, then picks them. The next year they perform near average. He had not accounted for the 190 funds that were discarded after random streaks.
expert.question: What best explains this?
options: Selecting winners after the fact exploits luck (data dredging)
Funds always fail after five years
expert.explanation: Among many funds, some will beat the market by chance; past luck does not predict future results.

expert.scenario: A company's average salary rises each year. A union says wages are stagnant for typical workers. Both statements are true because executive pay jumped.
expert.question: Which statistic best resolves the dispute?
expert.explanation: The mean is pulled up by outliers; the median reflects the typical worker.

expert.scenario: Policy A is argued for with: 'Opponents want chaos.' The opponents' actual position was a slower, phased rollout.
expert.question: Which fallacy is used?
expert.explanation: It attacks a distorted version of the opposing view.

expert.scenario: Because no one has proven that a supplement is harmful, a vendor claims it is safe.
expert.question: What is the flaw?
options: Appeal to ignorance: absence of proof is not proof of absence
expert.explanation: Lack of evidence of harm only shows it has not been tested or found yet.
